newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: High turnout reported in Ireland's election.
newsitem.headline: High turnout reported in Ireland's election.

text.p: Unofficial results from Ireland's general election should emerge on Saturday after opinion polls pointed to a tight contest between Prime Minister John Bruton's centre-left government and an opposition alliance led by Bertie Ahern.
But electoral officials said the final results under a complex voting system of proportional representation might not be announced until Sunday.

Polling stations stayed open until late on Friday and electoral officials said turnout by the 2.9 million voters was probably as high as 70 percent, compared with 62 percent in 1992 in the last elections.
It was the first time Ireland had voted on a Friday. Bruton chose the day over the customary Thursday date to allow people returning to their home constituencies for the weekend to vote.
Opinion polls before the election indicated that Ahern's centre-right alliance of Fianna Fail and the Progressive Democrats had a nine-point lead over Bruton's three-party "rainbow coalition."

But 16 per cent of voters were undecided, suggesting that neither bloc would win the 85 seats needed to ensure a majority in the 166-member parliament and would be dependent upon the support of smaller parties to govern.
The Greens, anti-abortion groups, independents and Sinn Fein, political wing of Northern Ireland's Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas, could be among the parties holding the balance of power.

Sinn Fein, tipped to win its first seat in parliament in modern Irish history, would use it to press its call for automatic entry into Northern Ireland peace talks, from which it is barred because of IRA violence.

Both Sinn Fein and the IRA want an end to British rule of Northern Ireland, a goal of the Irish constituution, but established Irish political parties have frozen contact with Sinn Fein until the IRA declares a ceasefire.

Bruton said he was confident that the voters would break with history and return an incumbent government for the first time in almost 30 years but Ahern's aides were equally optimistic that they would get back into power.

Fianna Fail, which promised to take a much tougher line on government spending than Bruton's administration, ruled with the Labour party of Foreign Minister Dick Spring until a row over legal appointments brought down the coalition in 1994.
Labour switched support to Bruton and, with the smaller Democratic Left, has been in power ever since but opinion polls suggest that Labour could lose a dozen of its 32 seats.
This would undermine Bruton, who urged voters to "Stick to the Rainbow" after it presided over record economic growth and job creation, earning Ireland's economy the title of "Celtic Tiger."
Both alliances are committed to ensuring that Ireland is one of the first countries to join the European Union's single currency and have brushed aside doubts about the project.
